slides.title: Globalisation of Law
slides.text: Lena Foljanty, 14 January 2026.

slides.title: Plan of the session
slides.text: What is globalisation? The institutionalisation of globalisation: the United Nations. The background: decolonisation after 1945. Economic globalisation and law. Law and development. The guiding question throughout: WHAT DOES GLOBALISATION MEAN FOR THE FIELD OF LAW?

slides.title: What is globalisation?
slides.text: A TERM USED SINCE THE 1990s TO DESCRIBE THE CURRENT AGE — so it is a word for a self-description, not a neutral label. Three components: the DENSIFICATION AND INCREASED IMPORTANCE OF GLOBAL NETWORKING; the EMERGENCE OF NEW GLOBAL ACTORS; and SOCIETIES SEEN NOT AS CLOSED BUT AS OPEN AND INTERACTING ENTITIES. The third is the one with consequences for law: a legal order built for a closed society regulates a territory, while an open and interacting one keeps producing questions its own state cannot answer alone.

cards.q: How does the lecture define globalisation?
cards.a: A term used SINCE THE 1990s to describe the current age: the densification and increased importance of global networking, the emergence of new global actors, and the view of societies not as closed but as OPEN AND INTERACTING entities. The last shift is what matters for law, since a legal order built for a closed society regulates a territory.

slides.title: Factors and conditions
slides.text: NEW TECHNICAL TOOLS FOR COMMUNICATION AND TRANSPORT — decreasing costs and increasing speed. INCREASING GLOBAL MARKETS. INCREASING MOBILITY OF GOODS AND PEOPLE, INCLUDING MIGRATION. And GLOBAL INSTITUTIONS. The first three are conditions the law does not create; the fourth is itself a legal construction — which is why the story divides into what law responds to and what law builds.

cards.q: Name the factors and conditions of increasing globalisation.
cards.a: New technical tools for communication and transport, with decreasing costs and increasing speed; increasing global markets; increasing mobility of goods and people including migration; and global institutions — the only one of the four that is itself a legal creation.

slides.title: Three patterns of globalisation in law
slides.text: The framework for both sessions, each with its example. FIRST, the CREATION OF SUPRA-NATIONAL LAW AND INSTITUTIONS — e.g. UN INSTITUTIONS AND CONVENTIONS. SECOND, the HARMONISATION OF LAW VIA LEGAL TRANSFERS, PARTLY AUTONOMOUS AND PARTLY HETERONOMOUS — e.g. DECOLONISATION AND DEVELOPMENT AID. Autonomous means the receiving state chooses; HETERONOMOUS means the transfer is imposed or conditioned from outside — the distinction is the whole moral difference between borrowing a code and being required to adopt one. THIRD, HETERARCHICAL NETWORKS BEYOND THE STATE — e.g. GLOBAL CONTRACT AND BUSINESS LAW. Heterarchical, not hierarchical: no level above the others, no legislator at the top.

terms.def: A legal transfer imposed or made a condition from outside, as against an autonomous one chosen by the receiving legal order.
Ordered without a hierarchy — networks of norm-production beyond the state with no level above the others and no central legislator.

cards.q: Name the three patterns of globalisation in law with an example of each.
cards.a: 1) Creation of supra-national law and institutions — UN institutions and conventions. 2) Harmonisation of law via legal transfers, partly autonomous and partly heteronomous — decolonisation and development aid. 3) Heterarchical networks beyond the state — global contract and business law.

cards.q: What is the difference between an autonomous and a heteronomous legal transfer?
cards.a: An autonomous transfer is chosen by the receiving legal order; a heteronomous one is imposed or made a condition from outside — the difference between borrowing a code and being required to adopt one, which is exactly the difference between post-war reception and aid conditionality.

slides.title: The United Nations
slides.text: The starting point is a FAILURE: the LEAGUE OF NATIONS. Then the DECLARATION OF 1942 BY THE ALLIES IN THE SECOND WORLD WAR — fighting against the aggressors, with a commitment 'TO DEFEND LIFE, LIBERTY, INDEPENDENCE AND RELIGIOUS FREEDOM, AND TO PRESERVE HUMAN RIGHTS AND JUSTICE IN THEIR OWN LANDS AS WELL AS IN OTHER LANDS'. Note the date: the human-rights commitment is made IN 1942, in the middle of the war, as a war aim. FOUNDATION OF THE UNITED NATIONS IN JUNE 1945, INITIALLY 50 MEMBER STATES, TODAY 193 — and the growth from 50 to 193 is itself the history of decolonisation, which is why the organisation's majority changed character without any amendment to its charter.

cards.q: What were the origins of the UN, and what does the growth from 50 to 193 members mean?
cards.a: The failure of the League of Nations, and the Allied Declaration of 1942 committing them 'to defend life, liberty, independence and religious freedom, and to preserve human rights and justice in their own lands as well as in other lands' — human rights declared as a WAR AIM. Founded in June 1945 with 50 members, today 193: the growth is the history of decolonisation, which changed the organisation's majority without any charter amendment.

slides.title: Universal human rights and the generations
slides.text: The UNIVERSAL DECLARATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS of 10 DECEMBER 1948, IN REACTION TO THE ATROCITIES OF THE SECOND WORLD WAR AND THE HOLOCAUST. And the scheme to reproduce: FIRST GENERATION — CIVIL AND POLITICAL RIGHTS; SECOND GENERATION — ECONOMIC, SOCIAL AND CULTURAL RIGHTS; THIRD GENERATION — COLLECTIVE OR SOLIDARITY RIGHTS; FOURTH GENERATION? with the question mark. The generations are not only chronological: they differ in who holds the right and what the state owes. The first requires the state to ABSTAIN, the second to PROVIDE, and the third is held by GROUPS rather than individuals — which is why the later slides read each generation back to the political constellation that produced it.

terms.def: First: civil and political (the state must abstain). Second: economic, social and cultural (the state must provide). Third: collective or solidarity rights (held by groups, not individuals).

cards.q: Name the generations of human rights and what distinguishes them.
cards.a: First: civil and political rights — the state must ABSTAIN. Second: economic, social and cultural rights — the state must PROVIDE. Third: collective or solidarity rights — held by GROUPS rather than individuals. A fourth is debated. They differ in who holds the right and what the state owes, not only in date.

cards.q: When and why was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted?
cards.a: On 10 December 1948, in reaction to the atrocities of the Second World War and the Holocaust.

slides.title: Decolonisation after 1945
slides.text: MAJOR CHALLENGES TO THE COLONIAL SITUATION AFTER THE SECOND WORLD WAR, driven by the CHANGE OF GLOBAL POWER CONSTELLATIONS WITH A NEW BI-POLAR CONSTELLATION IN THE COLD WAR — neither superpower had an interest in preserving the European empires. Two routes to independence: by TRANSFER OF POWER, e.g. FRENCH WEST AFRICA, or by SELF-LIBERATION WARS, e.g. INDOCHINA, ALGERIA, KENYA. The route matters for the law that follows: a transfer of power hands over the colonial state's institutions intact, while a war of liberation leaves a movement that has already governed territory of its own.

cards.q: By which two routes did decolonisation happen, and why does the route matter legally?
cards.a: By TRANSFER OF POWER (e.g. French West Africa) or by SELF-LIBERATION WARS (e.g. Indochina, Algeria, Kenya). The route matters because a transfer of power hands over the colonial state's institutions intact, while a liberation war leaves behind a movement that has already governed territory itself.
The change of global power constellations — the new bipolar order of the Cold War, in which neither superpower had an interest in preserving the European colonial empires.

slides.title: The speed of it
slides.text: THE END OF THE COLONIAL EMPIRES IN THE MID-1960s, WITH POST-COLONIAL STATE FORMATION. The numbers for Africa, and they are the thing to memorise: 1945 — 3 INDEPENDENT COUNTRIES; 1959 — 15; 1960 — 32. A continent's states created in a decade and a half, most of them in a single year. That pace is the reason for what follows: there was no time to build a legal order from nothing.

cards.q: Give the numbers of independent African countries in 1945, 1959 and 1960.
cards.a: 1945: three. 1959: fifteen. 1960: thirty-two. The colonial empires ended in the mid-1960s — and that pace explains why new states kept the former colonial power's law: there was no time to build an order from nothing.

slides.title: Bandung and the solidarity of the post-colonial states
slides.text: ANTI-COLONIAL INDEPENDENCE MOVEMENTS WERE OFTEN SOCIALIST OR COMMUNIST — IN REJECTION OF CAPITALISM AS THE ECONOMIC FORM OF COLONIALISM. Hold on to that clause: the political alignment was not incidental, it followed from an analysis of what colonialism had been. And SOLIDARITY AMONG THE (POST-)COLONIAL STATES: the AFRO-ASIAN CONFERENCES IN BANDUNG IN 1955, with FOLLOW-UP CONFERENCES UNTIL 1963, raising the CLAIM FOR INDEPENDENCE AND NON-INTERFERENCE.

cards.q: Why were anti-colonial movements often socialist or communist, and what was Bandung?
cards.a: Because they rejected CAPITALISM AS THE ECONOMIC FORM OF COLONIALISM — the alignment followed from their analysis of colonial rule. Bandung (1955) was the Afro-Asian conference, with follow-ups until 1963, expressing solidarity among the (post-)colonial states and the claim for independence and non-interference.

slides.title: The right to self-determination
slides.text: The decisive shift: THE DEBATE WAS DOMINATED LESS BY THE DEMAND FOR INDIVIDUAL RIGHTS THAN FOR THE RIGHT OF PEOPLES TO SELF-DETERMINATION, which was SEEN AS A PREREQUISITE FOR THE ENJOYMENT OF HUMAN RIGHTS — there was a STRUGGLE FOR ITS INCLUSION IN THE HUMAN RIGHTS CONVENTIONS. The result is ART. 1 OF THE INTERNATIONAL COVENANT ON ECONOMIC, SOCIAL AND CULTURAL RIGHTS (1966): 'ALL PEOPLES HAVE THE RIGHT OF SELF-DETERMINATION. BY VIRTUE OF THAT RIGHT THEY FREELY DETERMINE THEIR POLITICAL STATUS AND FREELY PURSUE THEIR ECONOMIC, SOCIAL AND CULTURAL DEVELOPMENT.' Note where it stands: ARTICLE ONE, ahead of every individual right in the covenant, and the holder is a PEOPLE, not a person. The Global South did not merely join the human-rights system; it changed what stands at the front of it.

cards.q: Quote Art. 1 of the ICESCR and explain its significance.
cards.a: 'All peoples have the right of self-determination. By virtue of that right they freely determine their political status and freely pursue their economic, social and cultural development.' Its significance: the holder is a PEOPLE, not an individual, and it stands as ARTICLE ONE, ahead of every individual right — the Global South's claim, fought into the covenants of 1966, as the precondition for enjoying human rights at all.

slides.title: Charter of the Organization of African Unity (1963)
slides.text: ART. II PURPOSES: '(c) TO DEFEND THEIR SOVEREIGNTY, THEIR TERRITORIAL INTEGRITY AND INDEPENDENCE; (d) TO ERADICATE ALL FORMS OF COLONIALISM FROM AFRICA; (e) TO PROMOTE INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION, HAVING DUE REGARD TO THE CHARTER OF THE UNITED NATIONS AND THE UNIVERSAL DECLARATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS.' ART. III PRINCIPLES: '2. NON-INTERFERENCE IN THE INTERNAL AFFAIRS OF STATES. 3. RESPECT FOR THE SOVEREIGNTY AND TERRITORIAL INTEGRITY OF EACH STATE AND FOR ITS INALIENABLE RIGHT TO INDEPENDENT EXISTENCE. 6. ABSOLUTE DEDICATION TO THE TOTAL EMANCIPATION OF THE AFRICAN TERRITORIES WHICH ARE STILL DEPENDENT.' Two things to notice. TERRITORIAL INTEGRITY means the COLONIAL BORDERS are kept — the new states guaranteed each other the frontiers the empires had drawn. And NON-INTERFERENCE cuts both ways: it is a shield against the former colonial powers, and it later stands in the way of any external response to what a member state does to its own population.

cards.q: What do the purposes and principles of the OAU Charter (1963) contain, and what is the tension in them?
cards.a: Purposes: defending sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence; eradicating all forms of colonialism from Africa; international cooperation with due regard to the UN Charter and the UDHR. Principles: non-interference in internal affairs, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, absolute dedication to emancipating the still-dependent territories. The tension: 'territorial integrity' preserves the COLONIAL BORDERS, and non-interference shields against the former colonial powers but also against any response to what a state does to its own population.

slides.title: Law in decolonised states
slides.text: DECOLONISATION GOES HAND IN HAND WITH NATION-STATE BUILDING, and therefore with a STRONG INTEREST IN STABILITY, ECONOMIC GROWTH, STATE FORMATION AND STATE UNITY. From it follows the NECESSITY TO CREATE AS QUICKLY AS POSSIBLE A WELL-WORKING LEGAL ORDER — and hence, OFTEN, STRONG CONTINUITY WITH THE LAW OF THE FORMER COLONIAL POWER. The paradox to state plainly: independence produced legal continuity, because the one thing a new state cannot afford is a period without a functioning legal system.

cards.q: Why did independence so often produce continuity with colonial law?
cards.a: Because decolonisation went together with nation-state building — a strong interest in stability, economic growth, state formation and unity — and therefore the necessity of a well-working legal order AS QUICKLY AS POSSIBLE. A new state cannot afford a period without a functioning legal system, so the former colonial power's law stayed.

slides.title: Legal transfer as the main tool
slides.text: How the continuity worked in practice: INSTITUTIONS OFTEN REMAINED; LOCAL ELITES HAD BEEN TRAINED IN THE LAW OF THE METROPOLIS; and OWN LEGAL EDUCATION PROGRAMMES had first to be built up. Then POSTCOLONIAL CODIFICATION WITH A METROPOLITAN MODEL: FORMER FRENCH COLONIES MOSTLY BASED ON THE FRENCH CONSTITUTION OF 1958, and FORMER BRITISH COLONIES GIVEN A 'STANDARD CONSTITUTION' ADAPTED IN COOPERATION WITH THE COLONIAL OFFICE. Note the second: the departing power supplied a constitutional template and helped adapt it — decolonisation drafted by the Colonial Office.

cards.q: On what models were post-colonial constitutions built?
cards.a: Former French colonies mostly on the FRENCH CONSTITUTION OF 1958; former British colonies on a 'STANDARD CONSTITUTION' adapted IN COOPERATION WITH THE COLONIAL OFFICE — the departing power supplying the template. Continuity was reinforced by surviving institutions and by local elites trained in the metropolis's law.

slides.title: The dual court system and customary law
slides.text: ABOLITION OF THE DUAL COURT SYSTEM WITH ITS OWN JURISDICTION FOR 'INDIGENOUS PEOPLE' — the colonial legal pluralism of the earlier lecture, dismantled. But in two different ways: PARTLY AN ATTEMPT TO ABOLISH CUSTOMARY LAW, PARTLY A CODIFICATION OF IT — and codifying custom is not preserving it, since writing it down fixes it and hands its interpretation to state courts. OFTEN A LIMITATION OF CUSTOMARY LAW IN ORDER TO CREATE A UNIFIED LEGAL ORDER FOR THE NEW NATION STATE. The consequences: ASSIMILATION OF INDIGENOUS CUSTOMS AND PRACTICES, and CUSTOMARY LAW OFTEN PREVAILING UNOFFICIALLY — driven out of the courts, not out of life.

cards.q: What happened to customary law in the new states, and with what result?
cards.a: The dual court system with separate jurisdiction for 'indigenous people' was abolished; customary law was partly suppressed and partly CODIFIED — which fixes it and hands its interpretation to state courts — and generally limited, to create one unified legal order for the nation state. The result: assimilation of indigenous customs, and customary law surviving UNOFFICIALLY — driven out of the courts, not out of life.

slides.title: Contextualising human rights
slides.text: The pay-off of the whole lecture, and the best single exam answer in it. THE SECOND GENERATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS REFLECTS CLEARLY THE MOVEMENT TOWARDS INDEPENDENCE AND DECOLONISATION — the claim of SELF-DETERMINATION, NON-INTERFERENCE AND SOVEREIGNTY. THE THIRD GENERATION REFLECTS THE ASSIMILATION OF INDIGENOUS CULTURES THAT TOOK PLACE IN THE COURSE OF NATION-STATE BUILDING — the PROTECTION OF INDIGENOUS CUSTOMS AND PRACTICES. So the generations are not a natural unfolding of an idea: each answers the political situation of the moment, and the third answers a harm caused by the second's own success.

cards.q: How do the second and third generations of human rights relate to decolonisation?
cards.a: The second generation reflects the movement towards independence — self-determination, non-interference, sovereignty. The third reflects the ASSIMILATION OF INDIGENOUS CULTURES that nation-state building itself produced, protecting indigenous customs and practices. The generations are not an idea unfolding: each answers a political situation, and the third answers a harm caused by the second's success.

slides.title: Law and development
slides.text: THE WORLD BANK AND THE INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND (IMF) AS GLOBAL INSTITUTIONS FOR FINANCIAL AID TO LESS DEVELOPED COUNTRIES AND COUNTRIES IN CRISIS, beside NATIONAL OR REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT AGENCIES. And the mechanism: CREDITS AND AID ARE OFTEN BOUND TO CONDITIONS — LEGAL AND ECONOMIC REFORMS, for example the IMPLEMENTATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND THE RULE OF LAW, AND ECONOMIC DE-REGULATION. This is LEGAL TRANSFER AS A MAIN TOOL in its HETERONOMOUS form: the receiving state formally chooses, but the alternative is no credit. The same instrument that carries the rule of law also carries de-regulation, and both arrive as conditions rather than as decisions.

terms.def: Credits and development aid tied to legal and economic reforms — human rights and the rule of law, but also economic de-regulation — making legal transfer heteronomous in form.

cards.q: How does development aid work as a vehicle of legal transfer?
cards.a: The World Bank, the IMF and national or regional development agencies bind credits and aid to CONDITIONS — legal and economic reforms such as the implementation of human rights and the rule of law, and economic de-regulation. It is legal transfer in its HETERONOMOUS form: formally chosen, but the alternative is no credit; and the same instrument carries de-regulation as carries the rule of law.

slides.title: Summary
slides.text: SUPRA-NATIONAL NORMATIVE REGIMES AND INSTITUTIONS ARE FORMED AFTER 1945 IN ORDER TO KEEP PEACE — and DECOLONISATION CHANGES THE POWER BALANCE WITHIN THESE INSTITUTIONS. LEGAL TRANSFER AS A TOOL PLAYS A MAJOR ROLE both in building new legal orders for decolonised nation states and in the context of development aid. And the conclusion, with its qualification: DESPITE THE FALL OF THE COLONIAL EMPIRES, THE LAW OF THE FORMER COLONIAL POWER AND OF THE GLOBAL NORTH REMAIN INFLUENTIAL — so there is a CONVERGENCE OF THE WORLD'S LEGAL ORDERS, HOWEVER WITH A LOT OF DIFFERENCES IN DETAIL. Convergence, not identity: the same formula as at the end of the lecture on the 19th century — spread is not sameness.

cards.q: Summarise decolonisation and supranational institutions after 1945 in three points.
cards.a: 1) Supra-national normative regimes and institutions were formed after 1945 to keep peace, and decolonisation changed the power balance within them. 2) Legal transfer was a major tool both in building the new states' legal orders and in development aid. 3) Despite the fall of the empires the law of the former colonial powers and of the Global North remains influential — a CONVERGENCE of the world's legal orders, but with many differences in detail.
